policy: These records describe evidence states, not translations. A known script, proposed sign value, language identification, and semantic translation are separate claims.

corpora.title: Voynich Manuscript
corpora.period: Fifteenth-century materials; text date remains a separate question
corpora.corpusScale: One illustrated codex with missing leaves
corpora.discovery: Documented modern provenance includes Wilfrid Voynich's acquisition in 1912; earlier ownership history is incomplete.
corpora.scriptState: Unidentified writing system or cipher
corpora.signInventory: Repeated glyph forms and scribal patterns are studied, but inventory boundaries depend on transcription conventions.
corpora.probableLanguage: No language identification has scholarly acceptance.
corpora.known: The physical manuscript is authentic and its parchment has been scientifically dated; it contains botanical, astronomical, biological, cosmological, pharmaceutical, and recipe-like visual sections.
corpora.unknown: Authorship, language, encoding method, and semantic content remain unknown.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Natural-language, cipher, constructed-system, and meaningless-text models remain research hypotheses.
corpora.strongestObjection: Physical dating and statistical structure do not validate any proposed reading.

corpora.title: Rohonc Codex
corpora.period: Date disputed; paper and watermarks require specialist assessment
corpora.corpusScale: One illustrated codex
corpora.artifact: Hungarian Academy of Sciences manuscript collection
corpora.discovery: Transferred with the Batthyány library to the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in the nineteenth century.
corpora.scriptState: Unknown script or cipher
corpora.signInventory: Large sign inventory reported; segmentation and sign variants remain disputed.
corpora.probableLanguage: No proposed language has consensus support.
corpora.known: The repository supplies a digitized physical manuscript.
corpora.unknown: Date, origin, script type, language, and meaning remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Proposals include ciphered religious narrative and constructed writing.
corpora.strongestObjection: Published readings do not have broad independent replication.

sources.label: Hungarian Academy of Sciences digital manuscript

corpora.title: Linear A
corpora.corpusScale: Multiple inscriptions on tablets, vessels, and other objects
corpora.discovery: Excavated at multiple Aegean sites beginning in the modern exploration of Bronze Age Crete.
corpora.scriptState: Sign repertoire is documented; some phonetic values are conventionally inferred through relation to Linear B
corpora.signInventory: Corpus sign lists distinguish syllabic-looking signs, logograms, and numerical or metrological signs.
corpora.probableLanguage: Often called Minoan; linguistic affiliation is not established.
corpora.known: Recurring signs, words, place names, accounting structures, and measures can be studied.
corpora.unknown: Most vocabulary and grammar remain unknown.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Related Aegean-script values permit cautious transcription of some sequences.
corpora.strongestObjection: Transferring Linear B values does not identify the language or yield secure translations.

corpora.title: Cretan Hieroglyphic
corpora.corpusScale: Small corpus on seals, bars, tablets, and other objects
corpora.discovery: Recovered from Bronze Age Cretan contexts.
corpora.scriptState: Recognized script with a catalogued but debated sign repertoire
corpora.signInventory: Sign identity and variants are studied across seals and administrative objects.
corpora.probableLanguage: Unknown; association with a specific language is unproved.
corpora.known: Material contexts and repeated sign sequences support analysis as a writing practice.
corpora.unknown: Phonetic values, language, and semantics remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Structural relations to other Aegean scripts are investigated.
corpora.strongestObjection: Graphic similarity alone cannot transfer readings between scripts.

corpora.title: Archanes Script
corpora.corpusScale: Tiny corpus, chiefly seal inscriptions
corpora.discovery: Recognized through seal material from Cretan archaeological contexts.
corpora.scriptState: Classification and relation to Cretan Hieroglyphic and Linear A remain debated
corpora.signInventory: Too small for a stable independent inventory.
corpora.probableLanguage: Unknown.
corpora.known: A short recurring sign group occurs on early Cretan seals.
corpora.unknown: Whether it is a distinct script stage, a formula, or another sign practice remains disputed.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: It may represent an early stage in Cretan writing.
corpora.strongestObjection: The corpus is too small for semantic decipherment.

corpora.title: Phaistos Disc
corpora.period: Minoan Bronze Age; exact date debated
corpora.corpusScale: One stamped clay disc
corpora.discovery: Excavated at Phaistos in 1908.
corpora.scriptState: Unique sign system with no accepted external corpus
corpora.signInventory: A finite set of stamped signs is visible, but sign count alone cannot determine language or meaning.
corpora.probableLanguage: Unknown.
corpora.known: The object has a spiral arrangement of repeated stamped signs on both faces.
corpora.unknown: Origin, language, function, and meaning remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: It may encode a linguistic text.
corpora.strongestObjection: A singleton without a bilingual anchor cannot support a demonstrable semantic decipherment.

corpora.title: Cypro-Minoan
corpora.region: Late Bronze Age Cyprus and Ugarit
corpora.corpusScale: Small corpus on tablets, clay balls, vessels, and other objects
corpora.discovery: Recovered principally in Cyprus, with tablet finds at Ugarit.
corpora.scriptState: Recognized Aegean-derived script family; internal grouping is debated
corpora.languageState: Unknown; one language cannot be assumed for every inscription
corpora.signInventory: Palaeographic variation complicates a single normalized sign list.
corpora.probableLanguage: Unknown; possible multilingual use remains open.
corpora.known: Material types, find contexts, repeated sequences, and graphic relations can be studied.
corpora.unknown: Secure sound values and languages remain unavailable.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Related Cypriot syllabaries may preserve some inherited structural features.
corpora.strongestObjection: Descendant-script values and graphic resemblance do not yield a secure decipherment.

corpora.title: Eteocypriot
corpora.corpusScale: Very small inscription corpus, including bilingual evidence
corpora.artifact: Inscriptions written with the Cypriot syllabary
corpora.discovery: Known from inscriptions associated especially with Amathus.
corpora.scriptState: Cypriot syllabary is readable
corpora.translationState: No generally accepted full translation of the corpus
corpora.signInventory: Uses a known syllabary; the obstacle is language rather than basic script identification.
corpora.probableLanguage: An indigenous Cypriot language is proposed, but identity and cultural implications are debated.
corpora.known: Text can be transliterated phonetically with the Cypriot syllabary.
corpora.unknown: Much vocabulary, grammar, and linguistic affiliation remain unknown.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Bilingual and formulaic evidence constrains parts of the corpus.
corpora.strongestObjection: Readable signs do not make the underlying language translated.

corpora.title: Eteocretan
corpora.corpusScale: A few alphabetic inscriptions
corpora.discovery: Recovered in eastern Cretan epigraphic contexts.
corpora.scriptState: Greek alphabet is readable
corpora.signInventory: Known alphabet; semantic interpretation remains limited.
corpora.probableLanguage: Possible continuity with Bronze Age Cretan language has been proposed but is not demonstrated.
corpora.known: Letter sequences can be transcribed.
corpora.unknown: Language affiliation, much morphology, and meaning remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: The inscriptions may preserve a pre-Greek Cretan language.
corpora.strongestObjection: Geographic continuity is not proof of linguistic descent from Linear A.

corpora.title: Indus / Harappan Script
corpora.region: Indus Valley and connected trade networks
corpora.period: Primarily third to early second millennium BCE
corpora.corpusScale: Thousands of short inscriptions, chiefly seals and sealings
corpora.discovery: Recovered at Harappan sites and in connected regions.
corpora.scriptState: Sign system documented; its precise linguistic status is debated
corpora.signInventory: Sign inventories vary with decisions about allographs and damage.
corpora.probableLanguage: Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Munda, and other proposals remain hypotheses.
corpora.known: The inscriptions are short, patterned, and materially associated with Indus civilization contexts.
corpora.unknown: Language, sign values, reading direction in every case, and semantic content remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Many scholars treat the signs as a linguistic writing system with structured sequences.
corpora.strongestObjection: The corpus lacks long texts and a bilingual, and non-linguistic-system arguments remain part of the debate.

corpora.title: Rongorongo
corpora.period: Surviving tablets documented in the nineteenth century; origins debated
corpora.corpusScale: Fewer than two dozen surviving wooden objects
corpora.discovery: Collected from Rapa Nui during the nineteenth century after major cultural disruption.
corpora.scriptState: Unique glyphic system; writing status and scope are studied
corpora.languageState: Rapa Nui association is plausible; encoded language and function are not established
corpora.signInventory: Catalogues depend on distinguishing variants and compound glyphs.
corpora.probableLanguage: Rapa Nui is often proposed; no continuous reading is accepted.
corpora.known: Surviving inscriptions use ordered glyph sequences and reverse-boustrophedon layout.
corpora.unknown: Full function, reading, chronology, and semantic content remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Some sequences may encode recitations, names, calendars, or genealogies.
corpora.strongestObjection: Reported oral identifications do not supply a repeatable sign-by-sign decipherment.

corpora.title: Proto-Elamite
corpora.period: Late fourth to early third millennium BCE
corpora.corpusScale: About 1,700 administrative tablets in the reviewed overview
corpora.discovery: Excavated at Susa and other Iranian sites.
corpora.scriptState: Structured administrative notation with partly understood numerical and commodity systems
corpora.signValuesState: Some numerical, metrological, and contextual functions understood
corpora.languageState: Underlying language and phonetic values remain unknown
corpora.translationState: Partial administrative interpretation; no full linguistic translation
corpora.signInventory: Hundreds of signs with continuing palaeographic normalization.
corpora.probableLanguage: No securely identified spoken language.
corpora.known: Document structure, numerical systems, commodities, and personnel categories can often be analyzed.
corpora.unknown: Phonetic reading, names, and full semantics remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Administrative regularities allow partial semantic reconstruction without a phonetic decipherment.
corpora.strongestObjection: Interpreting accounting structure is not equivalent to translating sentences.

corpora.title: Byblos / Pseudo-Hieroglyphic Script
corpora.corpusScale: Tiny corpus on bronze and stone
corpora.discovery: Excavated at Byblos in twentieth-century fieldwork.
corpora.scriptState: Recognized distinct sign system
corpora.languageState: Unknown; Semitic proposals are not accepted decipherments
corpora.signInventory: Small corpus prevents robust frequency validation.
corpora.probableLanguage: A Semitic language is often proposed but remains unproved.
corpora.known: The inscriptions are materially attested and can be compared structurally.
corpora.unknown: Sound values, language, and meaning remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Some analyses propose syllabic structure and West Semitic language.
corpora.strongestObjection: Assuming the language in advance permits non-unique readings in a tiny corpus.

sources.label: AUB publication of a claimed decipherment

corpora.title: Meroitic
corpora.period: First millennium BCE to first millennium CE
corpora.corpusScale: Substantial inscription corpus
corpora.discovery: Documented across Kushite archaeological contexts.
corpora.scriptState: Script signs and approximate sound values are known
corpora.languageState: Partially understood; affiliation and vocabulary remain limited
corpora.translationState: Names and recurring formulae can be read; many texts cannot be semantically translated
corpora.signInventory: Alphabetic and syllabic signs are catalogued.
corpora.probableLanguage: Meroitic; broader linguistic affiliation remains debated.
corpora.known: Royal names, some titles, sound values, and recurring elements are identifiable.
corpora.unknown: Large parts of vocabulary and grammar remain unclear.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Comparative work and formulaic contexts support incremental lexical interpretation.
corpora.strongestObjection: Phonetic reading without lexical understanding does not yield a full translation.

corpora.title: Iberian
corpora.corpusScale: Large inscription corpus in several signary traditions
corpora.artifact: Lead plaques, ceramics, coins, and monuments
corpora.discovery: Recovered across pre-Roman Iberian archaeological contexts.
corpora.scriptState: Most script values are substantially understood
corpora.signValuesState: Largely known, with palaeographic and dual-signary questions
corpora.languageState: Iberian remains unclassified and only partly understood
corpora.translationState: Texts can be transcribed; continuous semantic translation is usually unavailable
corpora.signInventory: Northeastern, southeastern, and Greco-Iberian writing practices require separate treatment.
corpora.probableLanguage: Iberian; relationship proposals remain debated.
corpora.known: Personal-name patterns, some morphology, and coin legends can be analyzed.
corpora.unknown: Most lexicon and wider affiliation remain unknown.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Bilingual names and internal comparison constrain readings.
corpora.strongestObjection: A readable script and recognizable names do not supply full semantic access.

corpora.title: Southwestern Paleohispanic / Tartessian
corpora.corpusScale: Inscribed stelae and other objects
corpora.discovery: Recovered in southern Portugal and southwestern Spain.
corpora.scriptState: Sign values and signary structure remain partly disputed
corpora.signInventory: Signary variants and redundant vowel notation are active research areas.
corpora.probableLanguage: No securely identified language; 'Tartessian' naming does not decide linguistic identity.
corpora.known: Repeated formulae and sign distributions can be studied.
corpora.unknown: Many values, language identity, and full semantics remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Comparative Paleohispanic epigraphy supports partial phonetic analysis.
corpora.strongestObjection: Historical labels cannot substitute for linguistic proof.

corpora.title: Khitan Large Script
corpora.corpusScale: Monumental and funerary inscriptions
corpora.discovery: Modern scholarly study followed discoveries of Khitan inscriptions in the twentieth century.
corpora.scriptState: Recognized logographic system with some identified values
corpora.translationState: Partial readings; no complete general decipherment
corpora.signInventory: Character lists remain incompletely interpreted.
corpora.probableLanguage: Khitan.
corpora.known: Names, titles, dates, and repeated formulae provide anchors.
corpora.unknown: Many characters and ordinary vocabulary remain unread.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Parallel historical formulae and personal names support incremental readings.
corpora.strongestObjection: Chinese-looking form does not authorize Chinese readings.

sources.label: Cambridge MIASU century of Khitan-script study

corpora.title: Khitan Small Script
corpora.corpusScale: Funerary and monumental inscriptions
corpora.discovery: A major small-script inscription entered modern study in 1922.
corpora.scriptState: Mixed phonographic system with many identified components
corpora.translationState: Substantial portions can be analyzed; not fully deciphered
corpora.signInventory: Signs combine in blocks and require distinction between graphic and phonetic components.
corpora.probableLanguage: Khitan.
corpora.known: Names, dates, morphology, and recurring formulae constrain readings.
corpora.unknown: Many signs and lexical items remain uncertain.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Comparative Khitan materials and multilingual historical names validate some readings.
corpora.strongestObjection: Unverified extensions from known signs can overstate translation coverage.

sources.label: Cambridge MIASU century of Khitan-script study

corpora.title: Jurchen Unresolved Material
corpora.corpusScale: Known inscriptions and documentary fragments
corpora.discovery: Epigraphic material has been recorded across former Jin territories.
corpora.scriptState: Writing system identified; readings remain incomplete
corpora.signInventory: Known and unresolved character forms must be distinguished.
corpora.probableLanguage: Jurchen.
corpora.known: Historical language identity and some character readings are established.
corpora.unknown: Unresolved signs and damaged passages prevent complete readings.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Comparison with related languages and known titles supports partial interpretation.
corpora.strongestObjection: Later Manchu evidence cannot mechanically determine every Jurchen form.

corpora.title: Vinča Sign Debate
corpora.corpusScale: Signs on pottery, figurines, and other objects
corpora.discovery: Recorded at Vinča and related archaeological sites.
corpora.scriptState: It is disputed whether the signs encode language
corpora.signInventory: Catalogues depend on separating decoration, marks, variants, and intentional sign groups.
corpora.probableLanguage: None can be inferred until linguistic writing is demonstrated.
corpora.known: Intentional signs occur on Neolithic objects.
corpora.unknown: Whether they constitute writing, proto-writing, ownership marks, ritual symbols, or several practices remains debated.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Repetition and conventional form may indicate an organized communication system.
corpora.strongestObjection: Short and isolated marks do not demonstrate encoding of spoken language.

sources.label: Institute for Balkan Studies writing-status debate

corpora.title: Tărtăria Tablet / Sign Debate
corpora.period: Neolithic context; chronology and treatment complicate direct dating
corpora.corpusScale: Three small tablets
corpora.discovery: Reported from a 1961 excavation at Tărtăria.
corpora.scriptState: Whether the marks constitute writing is disputed
corpora.signInventory: A singleton group cannot establish a full signary.
corpora.probableLanguage: None established.
corpora.known: The tablets bear intentional marks and have a documented archaeological debate.
corpora.unknown: Exact chronology, relation to Vinča signs, function, and linguistic status remain contested.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: The marks may belong to a broader Neolithic symbolic system.
corpora.strongestObjection: Claims of Sumerian or other readable text lack secure contextual and linguistic demonstration.

corpora.title: Jiahu Sign Debate
corpora.corpusScale: Small set of isolated marks on tortoise shell, bone, and pottery
corpora.discovery: Excavated at Jiahu.
corpora.scriptState: Intentional signs; status as writing is unproved
corpora.signInventory: The marks are too sparse to establish a linguistic signary.
corpora.probableLanguage: None can responsibly be assigned.
corpora.known: Marks occur in excavated Neolithic contexts.
corpora.unknown: Function, relation to later Chinese writing, and linguistic status remain unknown.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: They may represent early symbolic practices relevant to the long history of signs in China.
corpora.strongestObjection: Visual resemblance to later characters across millennia does not demonstrate continuity or reading.

corpora.title: Cascajal / Early Olmec Writing Evidence
corpora.period: Early first millennium BCE context proposed
corpora.corpusScale: One inscribed stone block
corpora.discovery: Reported from Cascajal, Veracruz; archaeological context has been central to evaluation.
corpora.scriptState: Proposed early writing system; classification remains debated
corpora.signInventory: A single text cannot establish allographs or a complete system.
corpora.probableLanguage: No language is securely identified.
corpora.known: The block presents repeated incised motifs in an ordered field.
corpora.unknown: Reading order, language, function, and relationship to later Mesoamerican scripts remain unresolved.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: The repeated, sequenced signs may constitute writing.
corpora.strongestObjection: A unique object without a bilingual or larger contextual corpus cannot sustain semantic decipherment.

sources.label: Science publication of the Cascajal Block

corpora.title: Isthmian / Epi-Olmec
corpora.period: Late first millennium BCE to early first millennium CE
corpora.corpusScale: Small corpus including long monumental inscriptions
corpora.artifact: La Mojarra Stela 1, Tuxtla Statuette, and related inscriptions
corpora.discovery: Objects were documented from Veracruz and neighboring regions.
corpora.scriptState: Recognized writing system
corpora.signValuesState: A published decipherment claim remains contested
corpora.signInventory: Structural analysis can proceed without accepting disputed readings.
corpora.probableLanguage: Mixe-Zoquean is a major proposal, not an established result.
corpora.known: Calendrical notation and formal sign structure can be studied.
corpora.unknown: Most sign values, language assignment, and semantic readings remain contested.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: Justeson and Kaufman proposed readings based on a Mixe-Zoquean language model.
corpora.strongestObjection: Independent tests have challenged whether the proposed readings generalize.

sources.label: University of Oklahoma Press: The Isthmian Script
BYU report on a critical test

corpora.title: Linear Elamite
corpora.corpusScale: Small corpus of monumental and object inscriptions
corpora.discovery: Recovered from Susa and other Iranian contexts.
corpora.scriptState: A substantial decipherment has been proposed and remains under scholarly evaluation
corpora.signValuesState: Many proposed values; acceptance is not uniform
corpora.translationState: Proposed readings exist; Atlas does not treat all as settled
corpora.signInventory: Corpus expansion through newly documented inscriptions affects evaluation.
corpora.probableLanguage: Elamite is the principal proposal.
corpora.known: Proper names and comparisons with cuneiform Elamite provide potential anchors.
corpora.unknown: The acceptance and reproducibility of the full value system remain debated.
corpora.strongestHypothesis: A 2022 decipherment argues that Linear Elamite records Elamite with a largely phonetic system.
corpora.strongestObjection: Individual sign values, corpus readings, and the degree of decipherment require continuing independent review.

hypotheses.method: Statistical structure, palaeography, and proposed cipher analysis
hypotheses.claimedReadings: No reading accepted by the field
hypotheses.criticism: Many incompatible models fit selected features without predicting unseen text.

hypotheses.criticism: Methods do not produce a uniquely reproducible reading across the manuscript.

hypotheses.proposedSignValues: Some conventional values transferred cautiously from related Linear B signs
hypotheses.claimedReadings: Partial phonetic transcription, not semantic translation
hypotheses.criticism: Shared form does not guarantee identical value, and the language remains unknown.
hypotheses.confidence: Moderate for limited sign correspondences; low for translation

hypotheses.method: Rebus, linguistic comparison, and distributional analysis
hypotheses.criticism: Short texts and unconstrained rebus choices permit non-unique readings.
Other statistical studies find structured ordering compatible with language-like systems.

hypotheses.method: Frequency, comparative Semitic morphology, and Egyptian/Phoenician comparison
hypotheses.peerReviewStatus: Published monograph; not accepted as a field-wide decipherment
hypotheses.criticism: The language assumption and tiny corpus underdetermine the values.

hypotheses.method: Calendrics, structural comparison, and proposed linguistic readings
hypotheses.claimedReadings: Narrative readings of La Mojarra and related inscriptions
hypotheses.criticism: Critics report that the system does not reliably read independent inscriptions.
hypotheses.confidence: Low to moderate for some structural observations; low for continuous translation

hypotheses.publication: The Decipherment of Linear Elamite Writing
hypotheses.method: Proper names, inscription parallels, and sign comparison
hypotheses.bilingualAnchor: Parallel name and text evidence rather than a single complete bilingual
hypotheses.criticism: The extent and certainty of values and readings remain debated.

hypotheses.proponent: Proponents of 'Old European' or Danube writing
hypotheses.method: Sign catalogues, recurrence, and contextual comparison
hypotheses.claimedReadings: Usually system-level claims rather than repeatable translations
hypotheses.criticism: Many marks are isolated and may be ownership, ritual, or decorative signs rather than language encoding.

hypotheses.proponent: Some researchers discussing early sign traditions
hypotheses.criticism: Large chronological gaps and a sparse corpus make direct script continuity unproved.

hypotheses.method: Oral accounts, repeated sequences, calendrical comparison, and glyph catalogues
hypotheses.claimedReadings: Selected sequences; no full accepted translation
hypotheses.criticism: Historical disruption, small corpus, and uncertain oral testimony prevent unique sign-value assignment.
